stem: The flow of electric charge (through a wire) is called __________.
solution: Electric current is the flow of electric charge through a conductor.

stem: A closed path along which electric current flows is called an __________.
solution: An electric circuit is a continuous, closed path through which current flows.

stem: In a circuit diagram, a cell/battery provides the __________.
solution: A cell or battery is the source of electrical energy that drives the current.

stem: The device used to open or close an electric circuit is a __________.
solution: A switch makes or breaks the circuit, turning the current on or off.

stem: When electric current passes through a wire, the wire becomes hot. This is called the __________ effect of current.
solution: The heating effect of current occurs when current flowing through a resistance produces heat.

stem: The heating effect of electric current is used in appliances like __________.
solution: Electric heaters, irons, toasters and geysers use the heating effect of current.

stem: The special wire used in a heater that gets very hot without melting is made of __________.
options: nichrome (an alloy with high resistance and high melting point)
solution: Nichrome has high resistance and a high melting point, so it heats up strongly without melting.

stem: The filament of an electric bulb glows because of the __________ effect of current.
solution: Current heats the bulb's filament until it becomes white-hot and gives out light — the heating effect.

stem: The filament of an electric bulb is usually made of __________.
solution: Tungsten is used for bulb filaments because of its very high melting point.

stem: A device that protects electrical circuits by melting when too much current flows is a __________.
solution: A fuse melts and breaks the circuit if excessive current flows, protecting appliances and wiring.

stem: A fuse works on the __________ effect of electric current.
solution: Excess current heats the fuse wire until it melts, breaking the circuit — the heating effect.

stem: A fuse wire is made of a material with a __________ melting point.
solution: A fuse wire has a low melting point so it melts quickly when the current exceeds the safe limit.

stem: When electric current flows through a wire, it produces a __________ effect around the wire.
solution: A current-carrying wire behaves like a magnet — this is the magnetic effect of current.

stem: A coil of wire wound around an iron piece that becomes a magnet when current flows is called an __________.
solution: An electromagnet is a coil around a soft-iron core that acts as a magnet only when current flows.

stem: An electromagnet loses its magnetism when __________.
solution: An electromagnet is magnetic only while current flows; switching off the current removes the magnetism.

stem: The strength of an electromagnet can be increased by __________.
options: increasing the number of turns of the coil or the current
solution: More turns of wire and a larger current make the electromagnet stronger.

stem: An advantage of an electromagnet over a permanent magnet is that it can be __________.
options: switched on and off and its strength varied
solution: Electromagnets can be turned on/off and their strength adjusted, unlike permanent magnets.

stem: Electromagnets are used in devices like __________.
options: electric bells, cranes for lifting scrap iron and loudspeakers
solution: Electromagnets are used in electric bells, junkyard cranes, loudspeakers and many machines.

stem: In an electric bell, the electromagnet __________.
options: attracts an iron strip repeatedly, striking a gong to make sound
solution: The electromagnet in a bell repeatedly attracts an armature that strikes the gong, then breaks the circuit, ringing continuously.

stem: The needle of a compass placed near a current-carrying wire __________.
options: deflects, showing the magnetic effect of current
solution: The compass needle deflects near a current-carrying wire because the current produces a magnetic field.

stem: The discovery that an electric current produces a magnetic effect is credited to __________.
solution: Oersted discovered that a current-carrying wire deflects a nearby compass needle, revealing the magnetic effect of current.

stem: Which of the following is a good conductor of electricity?
solution: Copper is a good conductor; rubber, plastic and wood are insulators.

stem: Which of the following is an insulator (poor conductor of electricity)?
solution: Plastic is an insulator; copper, iron and aluminium are conductors.

stem: Two or more cells joined together form a __________.
solution: A combination of two or more cells is called a battery.

stem: In a torch, the cells are connected so that the __________ terminal of one cell touches the __________ terminal of the next.
solution: Cells are usually joined in series, positive terminal to negative terminal, to add their voltages.

stem: MCBs (miniature circuit breakers) are now used in homes in place of fuses because they __________.
options: automatically switch off the circuit and can be reset
melt and must be replaced each time
solution: MCBs trip (switch off) on excess current and can be reset, unlike fuses which must be replaced.

stem: In a circuit, the bulb glows only when the switch is __________.
solution: The bulb glows only when the switch is on and the circuit is complete (closed).

stem: The symbol showing a longer line and a shorter line represents a __________ in circuit diagrams.
solution: A cell is shown by a long line (positive terminal) and a short line (negative terminal) in circuit diagrams.

stem: Which of the following appliances does NOT primarily use the heating effect of electric current?
solution: An electric fan uses the magnetic effect (motor); irons, heaters and toasters use the heating effect.

stem: The heat produced in a wire increases when the __________.
solution: More current or higher resistance produces more heat in a wire (the heating effect).

stem: Why should we not touch electrical appliances with wet hands?
options: Water conducts electricity and can cause an electric shock
solution: Wet skin and water conduct electricity, increasing the risk of a dangerous electric shock.

stem: The safe practice regarding a fuse is that it should be rated __________.
options: for the maximum safe current of the circuit
for the lowest possible value that keeps blowing
solution: A fuse must be rated to the circuit's safe current so it blows before dangerous overload occurs.

stem: An electromagnet uses a core of __________ so that it loses magnetism quickly when the current stops.
solution: Soft iron is used because it magnetises easily and loses magnetism quickly when the current is switched off.

stem: A large crane in a scrapyard lifts heavy iron objects using an __________.
options: permanent magnet that cannot be turned off
solution: Electromagnets lift heavy iron scrap and can release it by switching off the current.

stem: Which of the following statements about a fuse is correct?
options: It melts and breaks the circuit if the current is too high
solution: A fuse is a safety device that melts to break the circuit when the current exceeds a safe value.

stem: Overloading a circuit by connecting too many appliances can cause __________.
options: overheating and fire due to excessive current
solution: Overloading draws excessive current, overheating wires and risking fire; fuses/MCBs prevent this.

stem: When current flows through a coil wound on an iron nail, the nail can pick up __________.
solution: The current turns the nail into an electromagnet, which can attract iron pins.

stem: The direction of current in a simple circuit is taken from the __________ terminal of the cell through the circuit to the __________ terminal.
solution: Conventional current is taken to flow from the positive terminal, through the circuit, back to the negative terminal.

stem: A device that converts electrical energy into light using the heating effect is the __________.
solution: An incandescent bulb's filament heats up and glows, converting electrical energy to light.

stem: The two effects of electric current used in an electric bell are the __________.
options: magnetic effect (electromagnet) producing motion and sound
solution: An electric bell uses the magnetic effect of current (via an electromagnet) to produce repeated striking and sound.

stem: Which of the following would increase the number of iron pins an electromagnet can hold?
options: Winding more turns of wire in the coil
solution: More turns (and more current) strengthen the electromagnet, so it holds more pins.

stem: Electrical wires are covered with plastic or rubber because these materials are __________.
solution: Plastic/rubber insulation prevents the current from reaching us, protecting against shocks.

stem: A battery is used instead of a single cell to __________.
options: provide more voltage/energy to the circuit
solution: Combining cells into a battery increases the voltage and energy available to the circuit.

stem: A circuit in which the current has a complete, unbroken path is called a __________ circuit.
solution: A closed circuit has a complete path, allowing current to flow.

stem: If the wire in a circuit is broken or the switch is off, the circuit is __________ and no current flows.
solution: An open circuit has a gap, so no current can flow and the bulb does not glow.

stem: Which of the following is the safest action if you smell burning near an electrical appliance?
options: Switch off the mains and inform an adult
solution: Switch off the power at the mains and get help; never pour water on electrical fires or touch live wires.

stem: The main purpose of a switch in a household circuit is to __________.
options: control (turn on/off) the flow of current to an appliance
solution: A switch controls whether current flows to an appliance by opening or closing the circuit.

stem: Which of the following correctly matches a device with the effect of current it uses?
options: Electric iron – heating effect; electric bell – magnetic effect
Electric iron – magnetic effect; electric bell – heating effect
Both use only the chemical effect
Both use only the heating effect
solution: An electric iron uses the heating effect; an electric bell uses the magnetic effect (electromagnet).

stem: In a torch, the electric cell converts __________ energy into electrical energy.
solution: A cell converts stored chemical energy into electrical energy to drive the current.

stem: Which of the following will make an electromagnet stronger?
options: Increasing the current through the coil
solution: Increasing the current (or the number of turns) makes an electromagnet stronger.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Electric Current and its Effects' is that:
options: electric current produces heating and magnetic effects, which are used in devices like heaters, bulbs, fuses, electromagnets and bells
solution: The chapter explains the heating and magnetic effects of electric current and their applications in everyday devices.
